prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

right.text: A flat surface of a 3D shape
A line where two faces meet
A flat shape that folds up to make a 3D shape
The shape you see when you slice straight through a solid

hints: Picture a cardboard box. The flat sides, the folds and the corners each have a name.
solution: Face: a flat surface. Edge: where two faces meet. Vertex: a corner. Net: a flat shape that folds into a solid. Cross-section: the shape of a slice through a solid.

prompt: Which 3D shape has 6 faces that are all squares?

feedback.b: A square-based pyramid has only one square face. The other four are triangles.
feedback.c: A triangular prism has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles.
feedback.d: A hexagonal prism has 2 hexagons and 6 rectangles.

hints: Think of a dice.
solution: A **cube** has 6 faces, and every one is a square.

prompt: Which of these everyday objects is shaped like a prism?

feedback.b: A ball is a sphere. It has a curved surface and no flat faces.
feedback.c: A cone has a curved surface, so it isn’t a prism.
feedback.d: A party hat is a cone shape, with a curved surface.

hints: A prism has two matching ends joined by flat rectangles.
solution: A **tissue box** is a rectangular prism: two matching rectangle ends joined by rectangles. The other objects have curved surfaces.

prompt: Which shapes are faces of a **pentagonal prism**? Select all that apply.
hints: A prism is named after the shape of its two ends.
What shape are the faces that join the two ends of any prism?
solution: A pentagonal prism has 2 **pentagon** ends joined by 5 **rectangles**. It has no triangles, hexagons or circles.

prompt: Kai says a square-based pyramid has 8 edges: 4 around the base and 4 going up to the top. Grace says it has 5 edges. Who is right?

feedback.b: A square-based pyramid has 5 faces and 5 vertices. Grace may have counted those instead of the edges.
feedback.c: 12 is the number of edges of a cube.
feedback.d: That only counts the edges around the base. Don’t forget the sloping edges.

hints: Count the edges around the base first, then the edges going up to the top point.
solution: **Kai** is right. There are 4 edges around the square base and 4 sloping edges up to the apex: $4 + 4 = 8$ edges.

prompt: A prism has two identical [[a]] joined by [[b]]. A pyramid has one [[c]], and triangle faces that meet at a point called the [[d]].
hints: Think of a tent (a prism) and a square-based pyramid.
solution: A prism has two identical **ends** joined by **rectangles**. A pyramid has one **base**, and triangle faces that meet at the **apex**.

prompt: A tent is shaped like a triangular prism, and it has a floor. Each face is cut from one piece of material. How many pieces are needed?
hints: A triangular prism has two triangle ends. How many rectangles join them?
solution: A triangular prism has 2 triangle ends and 3 rectangles (two sloping sides and the floor): $2 + 3 = 5$ pieces.

prompt: A net is made of 2 hexagons and 6 rectangles. Which solid does it fold into?

feedback.b: A hexagonal pyramid has one hexagon and 6 triangles, not rectangles.
feedback.c: A rectangular prism has 6 faces, and they are all rectangles.
feedback.d: Count the faces: an octagonal prism has 2 octagons and 8 rectangles.

hints: Two matching shapes joined by rectangles means it is a prism.
The two matching shapes are the ends. What are they?
solution: Two matching hexagon ends joined by 6 rectangles make a **hexagonal prism**.

prompt: A tissue box is a rectangular prism. How many edges does it have?
hints: Count the edges around the top, around the bottom, and going up the sides.
solution: 4 edges around the top, 4 around the bottom and 4 joining them: $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ edges.

prompt:
Ella is making a model of a hexagonal pyramid. She uses straws for the edges and balls of plasticine for the vertices. How many of each does she need?

Straws: [[s]]

Balls of plasticine: [[b]]
hints: The base is a hexagon, with 6 edges and 6 corners.
Then there are the edges going up to the apex, and the apex itself.
solution:
Edges: 6 around the base and 6 up to the apex, so **12 straws**.

Vertices: 6 on the base and 1 at the apex, so **7 balls**.

prompt: What do we call a flat shape that can be folded up to make a 3D shape?
hints: It is also the name of something used for fishing.
solution: It is called a **net**.

prompt: Which solid has the same cross-section all the way along when you slice it parallel to its ends?

feedback.b: Slices of a pyramid get smaller towards the apex.
feedback.c: Slices of a pyramid get smaller towards the apex.
feedback.d: Slices of a ball are circles of different sizes.

hints: Imagine slicing it like a loaf of bread. Is every slice the same?
solution: A **prism** has the same cross-section all the way along. Every slice of a triangular prism is the same triangle. Slices of a pyramid or a ball change size.

prompt: A net for a hexagonal pyramid has [[a]] hexagon and [[b]] triangles.
hints: A net has one shape for each face.
How many sides does the base have? Each side has a triangle on it.
solution: A hexagonal pyramid has a hexagon base and a triangle on each of its 6 sides. So the net has **1** hexagon and **6** triangles.

prompt: Explain the difference between a prism and a pyramid.
modelAnswer: A prism has two identical ends that are joined by rectangles, so it is the same shape all the way along. A pyramid has only one base, and its other faces are triangles that slope up and meet at one point, the apex. For example, a triangular prism has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles, but a triangular pyramid has 4 triangles.

rubric.criterion: Says a prism has two identical ends joined by rectangles (or has the same cross-section all along)
Says a pyramid has one base and triangle faces that meet at a point (the apex)

hints: Think about the ends of each shape, and what shape the other faces are.
solution: A prism: two matching ends joined by rectangles. A pyramid: one base, with triangles meeting at the apex.

prompt:
A prism has 18 edges. How many faces and how many vertices does it have?

Faces: [[f]]

Vertices: [[v]]
hints: A prism with $n$-sided ends has $3n$ edges. Find $n$ first.
Then use faces $= n + 2$ and vertices $= 2n$.
solution:
$3n = 18$, so $n = 6$: it is a hexagonal prism.

Faces: $6 + 2 = 8$. Vertices: $2 \times 6 = 12$.

prompt: On a dice, opposite faces add up to 7. This is a net for a dice, with some of the numbers filled in. What number should go on the face marked X?

figure.alt: A cube net: a row of four squares with one square above and one below the second square. The row reads 1, 2, blank, X from left to right. The square above the 2 shows 3, and the square below the 2 is blank.

hints: In a straight line of three squares, the first and third end up opposite each other.
Which numbered square is two places away from X in the row?
solution:
In the row of four, the 2 and X are two squares apart, so they end up opposite each other on the dice.

Opposite faces add to 7, so $X = 7 - 2 = 5$.

prompt: Which of these solids has the **same** number of faces as vertices?

feedback.b: A cube has 6 faces but 8 vertices.
feedback.c: A triangular prism has 5 faces but 6 vertices.
feedback.d: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces but 10 vertices.

hints: Count the faces and the vertices of each solid.
For a pyramid with an $n$-sided base, both numbers are $n + 1$.
solution: A square-based pyramid has 5 faces (1 square and 4 triangles) and 5 vertices (4 on the base and the apex). In fact every pyramid has the same number of faces as vertices: $n + 1$.

prompt: Sione glues 3 cubes together in a straight row to make one long box shape. How many edges does the new shape have?
hints: What kind of 3D shape is the long box?
The glued faces are now inside the shape, so their edges are not edges any more.
solution: The new shape is a rectangular prism (a long box). Every rectangular prism has 4 edges around each end and 4 joining them, so it has **12** edges, the same as one cube. (It is not $3 \times 12 = 36$, because the glued faces are hidden inside.)

prompt: Explain why a net of six squares with a 2 by 2 block of squares in it can never fold into a cube.
modelAnswer: In a 2 by 2 block, four squares all meet at one point in the middle. When a cube is folded, only three faces meet at each corner (vertex). So the four squares around that point can’t all fit: two of them would end up on top of each other, and another face of the cube would be left open.

rubric.criterion: Says that only three faces of a cube meet at each corner (vertex)
Explains that four squares meeting at one point can’t fold to fit, so two would overlap and a face would be missing

hints: Look at the point in the middle of a 2 by 2 block. How many squares meet there?
How many faces meet at each corner of a cube?
solution: Four squares meet at the centre of a 2 by 2 block, but only three faces meet at any corner of a cube. Folding would force two squares onto the same face, leaving one face open.

prompt: A prism and a pyramid each have 12 edges. How many faces do they have **altogether**?
hints: Prism: $3n$ edges. Pyramid: $2n$ edges. Find $n$ for each one.
Then use faces $= n + 2$ for the prism and $n + 1$ for the pyramid.
solution:
Prism: $3n = 12$, so $n = 4$. It is a rectangular prism with $4 + 2 = 6$ faces.

Pyramid: $2n = 12$, so $n = 6$. It is a hexagonal pyramid with $6 + 1 = 7$ faces.

Altogether: $6 + 7 = 13$ faces.
